## The Problem: Adult Literacy in Eastwood

**[CLARITY OF PROBLEM]**

Low adult literacy is both a cause and a consequence of generational poverty. Adults who cannot read above a functional level struggle to secure stable employment, navigate healthcare systems, support their children's education, and participate fully in civic life. Nationally, 21% of U.S. adults read at or below a sixth-grade level (National Center for Education Statistics, [YEAR]), but in the Eastwood neighborhood of [City], the crisis is significantly more acute. According to the [County] Literacy Survey (2022), 23% of Eastwood adults read below a sixth-grade level — a rate that has remained virtually unchanged over the past [X] years despite broader statewide gains [SOURCE, YEAR]. Without targeted intervention, this cycle will persist, limiting economic mobility for thousands of residents and deepening disparities that ripple across education, health, and workforce systems.

**[DATA — LOCAL VS. NATIONAL COMPARISON]**

The consequences of low literacy in Eastwood are measurable and cascading. The neighborhood's median household income is $[X], roughly [X]% below the citywide median [SOURCE, YEAR]. Unemployment stands at [X]%, compared with [X]% for [City] overall [SOURCE, YEAR]. Health outcomes mirror this pattern: Eastwood residents report higher rates of [chronic condition] and are [X] times more likely to visit the emergency room for preventable conditions than residents in adjacent neighborhoods [SOURCE, YEAR]. Research consistently links low literacy to poorer health literacy, lower medication adherence, and higher healthcare costs (Berkman et al., Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, [YEAR]).

**[TARGET POPULATION]**

The burden falls disproportionately on [demographic group(s)], who make up [X]% of Eastwood's adult population and [X]% of those reading below a sixth-grade level [SOURCE, YEAR]. Many are [immigrants / formerly incarcerated individuals / parents without a high school credential — adjust to your population], facing compounding barriers including [language access / transportation / childcare / work schedules]. Women head [X]% of households in the target area [SOURCE, YEAR], meaning that a parent's literacy level directly shapes the educational trajectory of the next generation.

**[DATA — DEMAND AND SERVICE GAP]**

Demand for literacy services already far exceeds supply. Last year, [Organization] served 120 adults through its [program name], yet 200 additional residents remain on a waiting list — a gap that has grown by [X]% since [YEAR]. No other provider within a [X]-mile radius offers [comparable service] for this population [SOURCE or internal scan, YEAR]. The unmet need is not hypothetical; it is documented, growing, and urgent.

**[DATA — INTERGENERATIONAL IMPACT]**

The effects of adult illiteracy extend into Eastwood's schools. School absenteeism in the neighborhood is 12% higher than the district average ([City] School District Annual Report, 2023), and third-grade reading proficiency — a widely recognized predictor of long-term academic success — lags [X] percentage points behind the district benchmark [SOURCE, YEAR]. Parents who cannot read to their children or help with homework contribute to a cycle in which educational disadvantage is inherited rather than overcome. By investing in adult literacy now, this project addresses root causes that no amount of child-focused programming alone can resolve.

**[COMMUNITY VOICE]**

Eastwood residents themselves affirm this priority. In a [YEAR] community needs assessment conducted by [Organization / partner], [X]% of respondents ranked literacy and education as their top concern, and [X]% reported that limited reading skills had prevented them from [specific action: applying for a job, understanding a lease, helping a child with homework] in the past year. As one resident stated, "[Direct quote — brief, anonymized]." These voices ground our program design and ensure that the intervention reflects the community's own understanding of the problem.

## 3 Suggested Sources to Pull

1. **American Community Survey (ACS), 5-Year Estimates, Census Tract Level**
Pull median household income, unemployment rate, educational attainment, poverty rate, female-headed households, and language spoken at home for the specific Eastwood census tract(s). This gives you hyper-local demographic and economic data with federal credibility.
*Access: data.census.gov → filter by tract*

2. **[City/County] Community Health Needs Assessment (CHNA)**
Most hospitals and local health departments publish these every three years. Pull health literacy rates, chronic disease prevalence, ER utilization, and insurance status for Eastwood or its zip code. This backs up paragraphs on health consequences.
*Access: Local health department website or partner hospital*

3. **[State] Department of Education School Report Card Data**
Pull third-grade reading/ELA proficiency, chronic absenteeism, and graduation rates for the Eastwood-area elementary and middle schools. School-level data is more compelling than district averages and strengthens the intergenerational argument.
*Access: State DOE data portal → search by school name*

# Section 4: Program Design & Activities — DRAFT

---

## Logic-Model Summary

**[Design]** The program operates on a clear causal chain. **[Design]** Inputs — grant funds, trained instructors, classroom space, and community partnerships — support three core activities: structured literacy instruction, digital skills integration, and family literacy workshops. **[Design]** These activities produce measurable outputs: [X] instructional hours delivered, [X] adults enrolled, and [X] family workshops held per year. **[Design]** Outputs drive four short- and medium-term outcomes: increased reading levels, improved digital competency, higher parental engagement in children's education, and stronger employment readiness. **[Design]** The long-term outcome is a measurable reduction in intergenerational literacy disadvantage across Eastwood. **[Link]** A one-page logic model is included as Attachment [X].

---

## Participant Pathway

**[Design]** Every participant follows a structured four-stage pathway: intake, core instruction, transition, and follow-up.

**[Activity]** **Stage 1 — Intake & Assessment (Weeks 1–2).** Staff administer the [TABE / CASAS / validated tool] to establish a baseline reading level. **[Activity]** Each participant receives an individualized learning plan with short-term benchmarks and a long-term goal. **[Link]** This step directly addresses the rubric's baseline requirement in the Outcomes section.

**[Activity]** **Stage 2 — Core Instruction (Weeks 3–26).** Participants attend two 90-minute small-group literacy sessions per week, for a total dosage of [X] contact hours over 24 weeks. **[Activity]** Groups are capped at [X] learners to ensure individualized attention. **[Activity]** Sessions are held at [Location — community center, library branch, school site] during [morning and evening hours] to accommodate shift workers and parents. **[Activity]** Concurrently, participants attend one 60-minute digital skills lab per week, embedded into the literacy curriculum. **[Link]** This dual-track model ensures that reading gains transfer to real-world tasks such as completing online job applications, accessing health portals, and communicating with children's teachers.

**[Activity]** **Stage 3 — Transition & Goal Completion (Weeks 27–30).** Participants complete a post-assessment using the same validated tool administered at intake. **[Activity]** Staff work one-on-one with each participant to develop a next-step plan: enrollment in GED preparation, workforce training referral, or advancement to a higher-level literacy cohort. **[Link]** This stage converts program outputs into durable outcomes by connecting participants to continuing pathways.

**[Activity]** **Stage 4 — Follow-Up (Months 9–12).** Program staff contact participants at 3 and 6 months post-exit via phone, text, or home visit. **[Activity]** Follow-up tracks sustained reading habits, employment changes, and engagement with children's schooling. **[Link]** Retention of contact addresses the evaluation plan's need for longitudinal outcome data.

---

## Core Activities in Detail

### Activity 1: Structured Small-Group Literacy Instruction

**[Activity]** Trained instructors deliver two 90-minute sessions per week using the [curriculum name, e.g., Wilson Reading System / Orton-Gillingham–based approach]. **[Activity]** Instruction follows a scope and sequence that moves from phonemic awareness through fluency to functional comprehension. **[Activity]** Each session includes guided reading, vocabulary development, and applied practice using real-world texts such as lease agreements, prescription labels, and school notices. **[Evidence]** [Curriculum] has demonstrated [X]% average reading-level gain among adult learners in [X] peer-reviewed studies (Author, YEAR; Author, YEAR). **[Evidence]** A [City/Region] pilot using this model showed a [X]-grade-level increase over 20 weeks among participants with similar demographics (SOURCE, YEAR). **[Link]** This activity directly addresses the 23% below-sixth-grade-level finding in the 2022 County Literacy Survey cited in Section 2.

### Activity 2: Digital Skills Integration

**[Activity]** Participants attend one 60-minute digital lab per week, facilitated by the Digital Skills Coordinator. **[Activity]** Content progresses across three tiers: basic device navigation, internet safety and email, and applied tasks such as online job searches and patient portal use. **[Evidence]** Adults with low literacy are [X] times less likely to use the internet for employment or health management (Reder, [YEAR]; Warschauer & Tate, [YEAR]). **[Evidence]** Integrating digital skills into literacy instruction — rather than teaching them separately — increases retention and transfer (UNESCO Institute for Lifelong Learning, [YEAR]). **[Link]** This activity responds to the employment and health-access barriers identified in Section 2.

### Activity 3: Family Literacy Workshops

**[Activity]** Once per month, participants and their school-age children attend a 2-hour Saturday Family Literacy Workshop at [Location]. **[Activity]** Workshops include shared reading, take-home book distribution, and guided activities parents can replicate at home. **[Activity]** Content is co-designed with [School District family engagement office] to align with grade-level reading standards. **[Evidence]** Family literacy interventions increase both parental reading frequency and children's reading scores (National Center for Families Learning, [YEAR]). **[Link]** This activity targets the intergenerational cycle documented by Eastwood's 12% higher school absenteeism rate (School District Annual Report, 2023).

---
